title: How do you network for consulting jobs without feeling awkward?
description: A kind, practical guide to networking for consulting: who to contact, what to say, good questions to ask, and how to follow up.
hook: You network for consulting by having short, curious conversations with people about their jobs, not by asking strangers for referrals. Send a specific, modest request, prepare good questions, follow up with thanks, and use what you learn in your application. Done that way, it stops feeling awkward, because you are simply learning something you genuinely need to know.
body:
Why it helps

  • You learn what firms are really like. Work type, staffing, travel, client contact and feedback culture differ, and websites rarely tell you.
  • You get specific material for "why this firm". A detail from a real conversation beats anything from a brochure.
  • You may get advice on the process from someone who went through it recently.
  • Sometimes, a recommendation. If someone offers to refer you or pass on your CV, that is a bonus, not the goal.

Networking matters most if you do not come from a university or background with strong consulting links. It is how you close the information gap.

Who to contact

  • Alumni from your university or previous employers. LinkedIn's alumni search lets you filter by employer.
  • People you meet at firm events, presentations and campus sessions. Ask for their details on the day and follow up within 48 hours.
  • Friends of friends. A warm introduction nearly always beats a cold message.
  • People one or two years into the job. They remember recruiting well and are often the most generous with time.

A short message that works

Name a real connection, explain why them, and ask for something small.

Weak: "Hi, I'm very interested in consulting. Could you refer me to your firm?"
Strong: "Hi Priya, I'm a final-year economics student at Leeds exploring consulting. I saw you moved from engineering into your firm's transport practice, which is a path I'm considering. Would you have 15 minutes for a call in the next few weeks? I'd love to hear how you found the move."

The strong version is easy to say yes to: it is specific, it flatters nobody, and the request is small. Keep it under 80 words.

Running the conversation

For a 15 to 20 minute call, a simple shape works:

  1. Thirty seconds on you: who you are and why you are exploring consulting.
  2. Most of the time on them. Good questions:
    • "What's a recent problem your team solved, and what did the juniors actually do?"
    • "What surprised you most when you joined?"
    • "How is work staffed in your office, and how much do you travel?"
    • "What skills mattered most in your first year?"
    • "What do you wish you'd known before you applied?"
  3. One question on preparation, if they seem happy to talk about it.
  4. Close on time. Thank them, and ask if there is anyone else they would suggest you speak to.

Listen for differences between firms. They become the substance of your why this firm answer.

Follow up

Send a thank-you the same day that mentions something specific they said. Write down what you learned while it is fresh. If you apply, let them know. If they offer a referral, send the role link and a concise CV, and do not presume they will act on it. You are building a relationship, not collecting names to drop into applications.

A simple plan, with numbers

Here is an illustrative plan for one recruiting season. You are targeting five firms and want two or three conversations at each, so 10 to 15 calls. If roughly one in three messages gets a reply, you need about 30 to 45 messages: 10 ÷ (1/3) = 30 and 15 ÷ (1/3) = 45. Spread over four weeks, that is 8 to 12 messages a week and three or four calls. Very manageable, and far better than 100 messages in a panic the week before a deadline.

Track each contact in the same sheet as your applications: name, firm, date contacted, date of call, what you learned and next step. How consulting recruiting works shows how this fits the wider funnel.

Common mistakes

  • Asking for a referral first. Ask for information; let the person decide whether to offer more.
  • Turning up unprepared. Read their profile and the firm's recent work before the call.
  • Overstaying. Finish at the time you asked for, even if it is going well.
  • Name-dropping in interviews. Use what you learned, not who you spoke to, unless it is genuinely relevant.
  • Going quiet afterwards. A two-line update when you apply or get an offer keeps the relationship alive.

Practise now

1. Rewrite this message: "Dear Sir, I am a hard-working student passionate about consulting. Please let me know about openings at your firm."

Show the answer

Make it personal, specific and small: "Hi James, I'm a second-year maths student at Bristol, and I saw you joined your firm's London office from our course two years ago. I'm exploring consulting and would really value 15 minutes to hear what your first projects were like. Would a call in the next couple of weeks work?"

2. The call is going well, and with five minutes left the consultant asks, "Is there anything else I can help with?" What do you say?

Show the answer

"That's kind. Is there anyone else in the office, perhaps in the healthcare team, you think it would be useful for me to speak to?" Then, if it feels natural: "And if I apply, would you mind if I let you know?" Do not ask outright for a referral.

Where to go next

Turn what you learn into a sharp motivation with our why consulting examples, and check your CV with our consulting CV tips before you start sending messages.
